identification.title: God of Every Grace
identification.notes: Written by Keith Getty, Kristyn Getty, Matt Boswell and Bryan Fowler; copyright 2023 Getty Music Publishing, Messenger Hymns, bryanfowlersongs and Be Essential Songs, administered by Capitol CMG and Essential Music Publishing; CCLI 7223235. Kristyn Getty writes that it began with a melody and lyric from Fowler, and that the four shaped it over a couple of months, prompted partly by the 2023 Nashville school shooting and by family grief. The Getty, Boswell and Papa recording appears on I Set My Hope on Jesus (2023); Shane & Shane recorded it on Modern Hymns. Reviewed as the song, not as any one recording. Matt Papa is a recording artist, not a credited writer.

claims.structuralNotes: Three verses, each followed by the chorus, with the chorus repeated again in a closing outro. Verse one refuses to let sorrow steal hope, because the gospel shines in weakness; affliction is counted as a source of wisdom and God as the true treasure. Verse two prays for strength to rise, recalls Christ bearing grief at the cross, and trusts him to lead to glory. Verse three looks ahead to the dawn of hope, God's mercy swallowing up pain, and the gathering of God's children in heaven. The chorus praises the God who counts tears and holds days, and sings through sorrow in faith. The voice is first person singular lament and trust; the chorus is a personal doxology, with a corporate heaven scene in verse three. God is named as the addressee in the title and chorus; Christ appears at the cross.

claims.claim: The gospel's light shows in weakness, and affliction can be counted as a source of wisdom, with God himself as the believer's treasure.
claims.subject: Suffering and God's purposes

claims.claim: The believer asks God for strength to rise and trusts him to lead through hardship to glory.
claims.subject: God's sustaining grace

claims.claim: Christ bore grief at the cross, so he knows and carries the believer's sorrow.
claims.subject: Christ's suffering and atonement

claims.claim: God's mercy will swallow up pain, and his children will be gathered in heaven.
claims.subject: Final hope and glory

claims.claim: God counts every tear and holds every day, so the believer can sing through sorrow in faith.
claims.subject: Providence and God's care

strengths.title: Trust in God through affliction
strengths.explanation: The song does not deny sorrow; it sings through it, grounding hope in God's character and purposes rather than in circumstances. Affliction is set under God's wisdom, which is the biblical way of facing it.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Afflicted but not crushed, treasure in jars of clay - the song's posture toward weakness.

strengths.title: A God who counts tears and holds days
strengths.explanation: The chorus rests the believer's comfort on God's attentive care, not on the singer's strength. It is a pastoral picture of providence that a grieving congregation can hold.
strengths.scriptureRationale: God keeping count of tossings and storing tears - the image the chorus builds on.

strengths.title: Christ the suffering one at the centre
strengths.explanation: Verse two places Christ bearing grief at the cross as the reason the believer can trust him in pain. The cross is the answer to suffering, not a decoration.
strengths.scriptureRationale: He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows.

strengths.title: The end of pain and the gathering in heaven
strengths.explanation: The last verse fixes hope on God's mercy swallowing pain and the gathering of his children, so lament ends in promise rather than resignation.
strengths.scriptureRationale: God wiping every tear and ending death and mourning.

doctrinesAffirmed: God's providence and care in suffering
Christ bearing grief at the cross
God's strength made perfect in weakness
Final hope: pain ended and God's children gathered
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. The song speaks of suffering as ordinary Christian experience and answers it with God's care, Christ's cross and the promise of heaven. It is a song of comfort and trust more than a statement of the gospel's full order: sin and the resurrection are not reached, and the atonement appears as Christ bearing grief rather than sin. That is an absence, not an error.

strengths.title: A steady, pastoral melody
strengths.explanation: The tune is steady and easy to learn, and the chorus returns often enough for a room to take it up by the second time through.

strengths.title: Fits seasons of grief and lament
strengths.explanation: Few modern songs give a congregation words for sorrow that still end in hope. It suits funerals, hard weeks and ordinary Sundays where people are hurting.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Published with E as the original key, and also in Eb. Test the chorus for a mixed congregation and lower it if the top is a strain.

range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The chorus returns after every verse and again in the outro, but each return follows a new stage of the sorrow-to-hope movement, so the same confession lands on changed ground.
communal.assessment: Congregational in form and gentle in delivery. The chorus is learned quickly and the verses move at a pace that suits corporate singing. The voice is singular, which suits the personal register of lament.

strengths.title: God addressed plainly
strengths.explanation: The title and chorus name God as the one who sustains, so the song is never about an unnamed comfort. Christ is named at the cross.

clarity.assessment: Clear in what it claims. Its picture language, tears counted and days held, is biblical and plainly understood. The gospel itself is implicit rather than set out, which is a matter of scope.

synthesis.summary: A modern hymn of suffering and trust: sorrow is not denied, affliction is placed under God's wisdom, Christ is remembered bearing grief at the cross, and the final verse looks to pain swallowed by mercy and God's children gathered. God is named and the claims rest on his character. It does not reach sin, the resurrection or the Spirit, and its voice is singular.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The God of all grace who restores after a little suffering - the song's title and theme.
Afflicted yet not crushed, treasure in jars of clay - the first verse's stance.
God's power made perfect in weakness - the gospel shining through weakness.
God keeping count of tears - the chorus's image.
The servant bearing griefs and sorrows - Christ at the cross in verse two.
Death swallowed up forever - the third verse's hope.
Every tear wiped away - the final gathering.

sources.title: God of Every Grace: The Story Behind the Song
sources.establishes: Co-writer Kristyn Getty's own account: origin with Bryan Fowler's melody, shaped over months by the four writers, and her description of the song's teaching on suffering. Not independent.
